David Lloyd George. The last Liberal Prime Minister and a decisive wartime leader who mobilized Britain for total war and then grappled with the peace.

Lloyd George rose from a Welsh background and radical Liberal politics to become Prime Minister at fifty-two, breaking the aristocratic mold that had previously dominated the office. His tenure from 1916 to 1922 as PM saw him reshape the state apparatus, challenge the German Empire, and navigate the treacherous postwar settlement.

As Prime Minister, Lloyd George reorganized the British government for total war, centralizing procurement, propaganda, and strategy in a small War Cabinet that sidelined traditional ministers. He negotiated the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 as one of the Big Three alongside Woodrow Wilson and Georges Clemenceau, helping to shape the postwar order and the League of Nations. Earlier, as Chancellor, he had promoted social reform through his People's Budget of 1909, which taxed wealth to fund old-age pensions and National Insurance, presaging the modern welfare state.

In 1922, Lloyd George created the Irish Free State, effectively granting dominion status to most of Ireland after centuries of conflict and partition. This was a historic reversal of Conservative policy. However, that same year, Lloyd George lost office to a Conservative revolt, signaling the Liberal Party's terminal decline and the rise of Labour as the principal opposition to the Tories. His political career reflected the turbulent transformation of British politics in the early twentieth century.
